title: How to ask for Belief Statistics without Distortion?
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Economics, National University of Singapore (NUS) and

detail.title: How to ask for Belief Statistics without Distortion?
detail.abstract: Belief elicitation is ubiquitous in experiments but can distort behavior in the main tasks. We study when, and how, an experimenter can ask for a series of action-dependent belief statistics after a subject chooses an action, while incentivize truthful reports without distorting the subject's optimal action in the main experimental tasks. We first propose a novel mechanism called the Counterfactual Scoring Rule (CSR), which achieves such nondistortionary elicitation of any single belief statistic by decomposing it into supplemental action-independent statistics. In contrast, when eliciting a fixed set of belief statistics without such decomposition, we show that robust nondistortionary elicitation is achievable if and only if the questions satisfy a joint alignment condition with the task payoff. The necessity of joint alignment is established through a graph theoretical approach, while its sufficiency follows from invoking an adaptation of the Becker-DeGroot-Marschak mechanism. Our characterization applies to experiments with general task-payoff structures and belief elicitation questions.

title: Is Causality Necessary for Efficient Portfolios? A Computational Perspective on Predictive Validity and Model Misspecification
affiliations: University of Reading

detail.title: Is Causality Necessary for Efficient Portfolios? A Computational Perspective on Predictive Validity and Model Misspecification
detail.abstract: Portfolio optimization is increasingly argued to require causally identified return predictors to avoid signal inversion and optimization failure. This paper reexamines this claim by studying when predictive signals yield viable efficient frontiers, even under structural misspecification. We show that causal identification is not necessary for portfolio efficiency within static mean-variance and closely related quadratic portfolio optimization frameworks. Instead, efficiency is governed by geometric sufficiency conditions on predictive signals: directional alignment, ranking preservation, and calibration. We formally decompose portfolio efficiency into these three components and show that miscalibration alone attenuates Sharpe ratios even when alignment and ranking are preserved. Robustness is characterized as smooth degradation rather than collapse, with explicit attenuation behavior and continuity of performance under increasing misspecification. The theoretical results are supported by simulations and empirical analysis. Empirical validation combines equity-based illustrations with a large global bond universe spanning multiple currencies, countries, sectors, maturities along the term structure, seniority classes, and credit ratings, together with high-dimensional stress tests, nonlinear data-generating processes, rolling-window analyses, covariance regularization, realistic portfolio constraints, and bootstrap-based statistical validation. Across these settings, optimization geometry remains well behaved whenever directional alignment is preserved. The results clarify the boundary between causality and portfolio optimization: causality may inform signal representation, but portfolio efficiency at the optimization stage is a geometric property conditional on a given representation.

title: Collaborative Governance and Ethno-Tourism Development in a Multicultural City: The Case of Makassar, Indonesia
affiliations: Universitas Negeri Makassar, Universitas Negeri Makassar, UNM and

detail.title: Collaborative Governance and Ethno-Tourism Development in a Multicultural City: The Case of Makassar, Indonesia
detail.abstract: Background The development of ethnotourism in Makassar City has considerable potential; however, its management practices remain largely partial and have not yet been optimally integrated. This condition is indicated by weak synergy among actors, insufficient promotion grounded in local identity, and limited supporting infrastructure within cultural areas. Therefore, a collaborative governance approach is needed to integrate the interests of government, cultural communities, business actors, and academics into a unified policy direction and collective action. Objectives This study aims to: (1) describe the implementation of collaborative governance in ethnotourism development in Makassar City; and (2) identify the supporting and inhibiting factors affecting such collaboration. Methods The research employs a descriptive qualitative approach. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, participant observation, and documentation review. Data analysis followed the interactive model of Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña, comprising data collection, data reduction, data display, and cyclical conclusion drawing/verification. Results The findings show that collaboration occurs through both formal and informal mechanisms, such as MoUs/cooperation agreements, FGDs, cultural forums, community deliberations, and interethnic dialogues; this pattern strengthens cross-stakeholder coordination. Key supporting factors include cultural richness and diversity, interethnic social tolerance, strong community cohesion, supportive government policies, and growing tourist interest in cultural tourism and authentic experiences. Inhibiting factors include limited budgets, uneven human resource capacity, differing understandings of the ethnotourism concept, dependence on external support, and community concerns regarding the negative impacts of tourism. Conclusion Collaborative-based ethnotourism development generates multidimensional positive impacts, particularly in strengthening cultural identity and appreciation, improving the local/creative economy, and maintaining social tolerance and harmony in Makassar City. Overall, collaborative governance is considered appropriate and relevant; however, its effectiveness should be reinforced through institutional strengthening, capacity building among actors, and sustained commitment across stakeholders.

title: Can Randomized Controlled Trials be a Discovery Process?

detail.title: Can Randomized Controlled Trials be a Discovery Process?
detail.abstract: Trends in development economics have led randomized controlled trials to be a popular method for investigating a variety of questions in developing economies. This chapter weighs significant arguments that RCTs are one of the best tools for program evaluation against criticisms of their internal and external validity. To resolve these debates, it then turns to discuss the implicit political economy of the process described by the 2019 Nobel Prize winners. Finally, to satisfy these and other institutional prerequisites for experimentation in a developing society to be productive, it argues that embedding RCTs and other forms of experimentation in a civil society is more likely to produce improvements in human wellbeing than embedding RCTs in a developmental state.

title: The Retirement Spending Smile Revisited: Cross-Sectional Patterns versus Within-Household Dynamics
affiliations: University of Southern Maine

detail.title: The Retirement Spending Smile Revisited: Cross-Sectional Patterns versus Within-Household Dynamics
detail.abstract: The "retirement spending smile" (Blanchett, 2014), a U-shaped pattern in the rate of retiree spending change, has shaped how advisors and retirees think about spending in retirement. We replicate Blanchett's analysis using RAND HRS/CAMS data (2001-2009) and extend it with panel econometric methods through 2021. Our central finding: the smile pattern appears when comparing different households at different ages, but is not statistically detectable when tracking the same households over time. This divergence may reflect cohort composition, period effects, survivorship, or other factors rather than individual-level dynamics, though the data do not permit a clean causal decomposition. In our replication, coefficient signs match Blanchett's specification, but 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for Age² and Age include zero – meaning the evidence for the smile's curvature is not statistically distinguishable from a simple linear decline. We also document that the ln(Spending) coefficient sign depends on whether spending is measured at interval start or end, an implementation choice not specified in the original. The central finding (smile attenuation in within-household analysis) is robust to survey weighting. For individual client projections, a constant real decline (~1%, with sensitivity around 0-2% annually) is a more defensible baseline than assuming a smile pattern.

title: Toggling the Defiers to Relax Monotonicity: The Difference-in-Instrumental-Variables Estimand
affiliations: Hiroshima University

detail.title: Toggling the Defiers to Relax Monotonicity: The Difference-in-Instrumental-Variables Estimand
detail.abstract: Standard instrumental variables (IV) methods identify a Local Average Treatment Effect under monotonicity, which rules out defiers. In many empirical environments, however, distinct instruments may induce heterogeneous and even opposing behavioral responses. This paper introduces the Difference-in-Instrumental-Variables (DIIV) estimand, which exploits two instruments with opposing compliance patterns to recover a point-identified and behaviorally interpretable causal effect without imposing monotonicity. The estimand yields a convex combination of the marginal treatment effects on compliers and defiers, with weights reflecting differential shifts in treatment take-up across instruments. When monotonicity holds, DIIV coincides with the standard IV estimand. The approach can be implemented using simple linear transformations and standard two-stage least squares procedures. Applications using replication data illustrate its applicability in practice.

title: Artificial Intelligence and College Major Choice
affiliations: and The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and College Major Choice
detail.abstract: This paper studies how the diffusion of artificial intelligence technology reshapes human capital investment. Using online job postings data from Lightcast along with American Community Survey data, we construct a measure of local AI labor demand shocks based on shift-share instruments. Higher AI demand reallocates the field-ofdegree composition of young college graduates toward AI intensive majors, such as computer science and engineering, and away from education and humanities, while there is no significant effect on overall college enrollment or college premium. Moreover, AI demand raises local income, with gains concentrated in higher-income areas, suggesting that AI can widen geographic disparities.

title: A Structural VAR (SVAR) based Approach to Calculating the Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) across Income Groups
affiliations: , The Central Bank of Bangladesh

detail.title: A Structural VAR (SVAR) based Approach to Calculating the Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) across Income Groups
detail.abstract: Here we have devised a new structural VAR (SVAR) based approach to measuring marginal propensity to consume (MPC) of households from different income groups. To be precise, we build structural VAR model with group-wise income and expenditure data of US households and perform impulse response analysis on the model to estimate the MPC of different income groups. Our analysis suggests that MPC values of US households belonging to bottom [0-20]%, [20-40]%, [40-60]%, [60-80]% and [80-100]% income group are 0.95, 0..81, 0.74, 0.71 and 0.35 respectively, which nicely converges with the existing theory of MPC that says, low income households have higher MPCs. Alongside conventional approaches of measuring MPCs, which involve OLS regression, instrumental variable, randomized control trial, natural experiment, variance decomposition etc., here we have developed a new methodology of measuring MPCs, which relies on standardized secondary data and provides reliable estimates of MPCs that nicely resembles to the existing theory.

title: A New SMP Transformed Standard Weibull Distribution for Health Data Modelling
affiliations: The University of Manchester, University of Louisiana at Lafayette and Nova Southeastern University

detail.title: A New SMP Transformed Standard Weibull Distribution for Health Data Modelling
detail.abstract: New methods of extending base distributions are always invoke to increase their adaptability in modeling real life data. Recently, SMP method was introduced but Weibull distribution is yet to be explored through this method. First, we provide updated review on SMP transformed distributions. We then proposed and developed another extended Weibull distribution through this technique named SMPtW. Importantly, twelve of its statistical properties - reliability measures, quantile function, moment, stress-strength, mean waiting time, moment generating function, characteristics function, renyi entropy, order statistics, mean residual life and mode, were derived and studied extensively. The hazard function has a decreasing, increasing and constant shapes. We found a relation between the quantile of SMPtW and that of SMP Pareto distribution despite their difference in density functions. We adopt the inverse transform approach in random number generation and through simulation we evaluate maximum likelihood estimates (MLE) performance of its parameters. The result showed that MLE is consistent all through. The performance of the distribution was then examined using health dataset compared with five similar distributions. The results showed that three parameters SMPtW performed best among the competing models.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a monetary system in which the US dollar is defined as a fractional claim on the aggregate equity of the 500 largest publicly traded US companies by market capitalization, with the fraction decreasing at a legislatively fixed annual rate. Building on Demyanov (2021), which introduced index-linked central bank rates and chain indexation of the economy, the system takes this logic to its conclusion by defining the currency itself as a fraction of the index, eliminating discretionary money creation entirely. The money supply grows through two channels distinguished by their inflationary properties: compositional turnover in the index, which is compensatory and non-inflationary, and the legislatively mandated decrease in the dollar’s equity fraction, which is the system’s sole source of inflation. Government revenue derives from three parallel wealth taxes—mandatory equity dilution on all business entities, the fractional decrease (the inflation tax), and a federal property tax on real property. The three taxes are set at a uniform rate, a design constraint that prevents wealth migration between asset classes and that is absent from prior wealth tax proposals. The equity dilution mechanism avoids the valuation, liquidity, and unrealized-gains problems that have historically blocked wealth tax implementation: public companies simply issue new shares, the market provides continuous pricing, and no entity is forced to sell assets or generate cash. The definitional identity between the monetary base and the index’s total market capitalization produces structural properties absent from both fiat and prior asset-backed monetary systems: the aggregate index cannot decline in its own unit, the government’s primary revenue streams are recession-proof by mathematical identity rather than empirical approximation, and the sovereign debt crisis mechanism is largely eliminated. We analyze the system’s behavior under normal economic conditions, overheating, recession, and financial crisis.

title: IP and Music: Harnessing Nigeria's Music Industry for Economic Growth
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: IP and Music: Harnessing Nigeria's Music Industry for Economic Growth
detail.abstract:
The economic power of music is more than art—it is big business.
Nowhere is this statement truer than in Nigeria, where music has become one of the country’s most valuable exports. A 2025 Spotify report reveals that Nigeria’s music exports grew by 49 percent over the past three years due to the Afrobeats boom. Additionally, recent report indicates that royalties generated by Nigerian artists on Spotify alone exceeded 58 billion naira in 2024. Likewise, a 2024 report by Statista indicates that music recording as well as motion picture accounted for roughly 154 billion naira of Nigeria's GDP in 2023. In the same vein, Nigerian artists like Rema, who broke Spotify streaming records with the remix of his song “Calm Down,” and Tems, who have won two Grammy awards, are breaking barriers and redefining the importance of Afrobeat on the global stage. 

However, behind the glitz and glamour lies a cancerous tumor that has spread across the Nigerian music industry: intellectual property infringement. The labours of music creators are being exploited, thereby depriving artists of their rights and consequently undermining fundamental financial growth and development in the industry. Against this backdrop, this essay examines how IP can help in transforming Nigeria’s music industry into a reliable driver of sustainable economic growth.

title: Statistical Analysis of Climate Change Impact on Macroeconomic Variables in Ghana
affiliations: University of Ghana - University of Ghana, University of Ghana, University of Ghana and University of Ghana

detail.title: Statistical Analysis of Climate Change Impact on Macroeconomic Variables in Ghana
detail.abstract: Climate change presents a cosmopolitan challenge with far-reaching macroeconomic implications, demanding immediate action. Thus, this study sought to offer a statistical analysis exploring the macroeconomic effects of climate change in Ghana using monthly observations from 2000 to 2023. By utilizing Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA), the study examined the statistical relationship between climate variables (represented by Global CO2 levels, temperature, rainfall, and humidity obtained from GMet’s 22 monitored synopsis stations) and key macroeconomic indicators (including economic growth rates, inflation rates, real effective exchange rates, and interest rates). The short-run and long-term impacts of climate change on these economic variables were assessed by applying Vector Autoregression (VAR). The observed pattern among the examined economic and climate metrics suggests a symbiotic influence, where fluctuations in these variables have interconnected impacts. Notably, the VAR analysis results disclosed that a 1% increase in relative humidity in Ada and a unit rise in temperature across Abetifi, Bole, Kumasi, and Tema weather stations are associated with adverse effects on certain macroeconomic indicators, particularly immediate and long-term interest rates and inflation rates, albeit with some degree of uncertainty. The study advises that strengthening Ghana’s economic resilience to climate change requires targeted investments in climate-smart agriculture and infrastructure, particularly in vulnerable communities. Prioritizing smallholder farmers through adaptation financing and insurance is critical. Integrating climate risk into monetary and fiscal policy, alongside improved data systems and research, will support responsive and inclusive planning.

While peatlands account for only 3% of the Earth’s surface, they store approximately one-quarter of global soil carbon, making them vital ecosystems for climate regulation. By applying Arturo Escobar’s post-development theory, originally rooted in Latin American discourse, this paper critiques the Western linear model of modernisation and its "productivist" understanding of progress. detail.abstract: This paper provides an overview of the law on the addition of vitamins and minerals to foods (‘fortification’) in the EU and three of its Member States: Denmark, Finland and the Netherlands.EU food law starts from the assumption that a normal varied diet provides all the micronutrients that a consumer needs. The addition of vitamins or minerals to the diet would rarely be needed. Mandatory fortification is absent in EU law and rare in the law of the Member States. Regulation (EC) 1925/2006 on the addition of vitamins and minerals and of certain other substances to foods, therefore, is mostly relevant voor voluntary fortification. Topics are addressed such as purposes of fortification, the nature and quantity of micronutrients added, and foods excluded for use as vehicles for fortification. Other topics of interest addressed in this paper are nutrition declaration and claims. Regulatory oversight is based on pre-approval in Denmark, notification in Finland and exemptions from a prohibition to fortify in the Netherlands.

detail.abstract:
Modern banking systems are constructed around an explicit objective of stability. Capital buffers, liquidity requirements, governance frameworks, supervisory oversight, and increasingly sophisticated technological controls are intended to reduce risk and prevent systemic failure. Yet despite repeated reform cycles, banking crises and near-crises continue to recur with notable regularity. This persistence raises a fundamental question: how do stability-oriented designs themselves become sources of fragility?

This paper examines banking stability not as a static condition, but as a dynamic outcome shaped by institutional design choices and system interactions over time. Using a conceptual and system-level analytical approach, it explores how governance architectures, incentive structures, and digital infrastructures interact to transform protective mechanisms into amplifiers of systemic risk. Rather than focusing on individual institutions or discrete regulatory failures, the analysis emphasises structural feedback loops that emerge across complex financial systems.

detail.abstract: For over two centuries, economic thought has been centered on the concept of "Utility." We have built global empires on the understanding of human psychology, assuming that value is a subjective feeling pursued in a world of scarcity. This paper explores the possibility that we might benefit from a different map-one grounded in physical reality. Value may not only be a psychological whim; it can be viewed as a physical struggle. Every economic system in history-from the grain ledgers of Babylon to the high-frequency trading of Wall Street-can be seen as a purposebuilt engine designed to navigate the laws of physics. Specifically, we address Friction. Prosperity, in this view, is not just about having "more." It is about Value Continuity: the ability to preserve the surplus we create and move it across the three irreducible walls of reality: Exchange, Time, and Space (ETS). By seeking to minimize these frictions, we may unlock the true potential of the human species.

detail.abstract: The prevailing pursuit of economic success is often simplified to maximizing Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth. This unidimensional focus, while powerful in measuring aggregate activity, has proven fundamentally inadequate. [5] It systematically fails to capture the essential components of true human well-being and resilient prosperity, specifically neglecting the importance of structural stability (R), institutional fairness (F), or technological capability (S). [2] The global financial crisis of 2008, the subsequent rise of systemic inequality, and the persistent vulnerabilities exposed by global health crises have demonstrated unequivocally that traditional economic models lack the diagnostic depth required for resilient prosperity. [3] Prosperity without resilience is merely volatility waiting to happen. [1] This book posits that a fundamental re-conceptualization of economic activity is required, one that shifts the focus from purely psychological motives (utility maximization) to the physical and informational frictions that govern the transfer and preservation of value. We introduce the ETS-RFS Synthesis, a master conceptual framework that redefines economic theory on transdisciplinary grounds. At its foundation, the Exchange, Time, Space (ETS) Constraints Theory asserts that all economic institutions and technologies are purpose-built systems designed to manage three irreducible constraints: Exchange (E), Time (T), and Space (S). [3, 2] The longterm, ethical goal of economic policy is then framed by the Real Free Sophisticated (RFS) Framework, which provides a tripartite, measurable diagnostic for achieving a balanced state of resilient well-being. [2] Crucially, this synthesis explores the dangerous shadow of relentless optimization: the Self-Consuming Efficiency Paradox. [4] This paradox reveals why the very success of minimizing the ETS constraints in the digital age leading to hyper-efficiency paradoxically degrades the human lives it seeks to serve, resulting in societal friction, stress, and burnout. [4] This manuscript, structured across four distinct parts, provides a universal blueprint for policymakers, technologists, and citizens. It aims to offer not just a new theoretical lens for understanding economic history and modern crises, but also a practical, balanced approach to building sustainable, humane economies.

detail.abstract: Does fair lending litigation impact mortgage lender decisions? Using a novel dataset of all fair lending legal actions from 1991 to 2023, we find that it does. In the wake of legal settlements for discrimination against Black borrowers, lenders significantly reduced denial rates for Black applicants. The reductions offset pre-litigation racial disparities in denial rates by litigated banks, relative to those banks' competitors. Origination rates for Black applicants also increased post-litigation. We further observe evidence of a spillover effect on the approval decisions of non-litigated banks operating in the same city as a litigated bank. Altogether, the evidence suggests that the enforcement of fair lending laws is an effective tool to reduce racial discrimination in credit markets.

This paper presents an experimental visualization cockpit designed to externalize the internal cognitive layers of a regime-adaptive market architecture. The cockpit is derived from the AlphaGen framework for autonomous regime-aware strategy evolution and is released as a frozen reference implementation (Experimental Cockpit v1). Rather than generating executable trades, investment advice, or performance claims, the cockpit exposes intermediate abstractions—market aggregation, trait inference, finite-state regime modelling, adaptive risk posture, and decision alignment—within a unified interface.

The system enables inspection of how market information propagates through a layered cognitive architecture, supporting interpretability, auditability, and architectural validation. The cockpit is demonstrated using Indian equity symbols solely as an illustrative case study. No broker connectivity, execution logic, or optimization objectives are included. The contribution of this work lies in demonstrating how regime-aware market cognition architectures can be made transparent and analysable through structured visualization artifacts.

title: Success, Status, and the Endogenous Origins of Decline

detail.title: Success, Status, and the Endogenous Origins of Decline
detail.abstract: Societies characterized by sustained prosperity and security exhibit a recurring cluster of outcomes across diverse social contexts-declining fertility, care-centered moralization, intensified moral enforcement, distributive polarization, and the weakening of containment and corrective mechanisms. These phenomena are typically analyzed in isolation or attributed to cultural change, ideological diffusion, or institutional drift. This paper proposes a unified, micro-founded theoretical framework that explains their joint emergence as unintended consequences of altered incentive and selection environments generated by sustained success. The model assigns causal priority to individual incentives, status competition, and sexual selection operating under relaxed material and reproductive constraints. Sustained prosperity and security reconfigure aggregate mating preferences, generating a directional selection bias favoring care-consistent traits that is amplified and stabilized through status competition. From this shared upstream transformation, two analytically distinct downstream trajectories emerge. The first is a normative-symbolic sequence in which care-centered signaling produces inversion of traditional status markers, crystallizes into moral values, and culminates in intensified enforcement practices. The second is a distributive-structural sequence in which mating-market concentration generates de facto polygyny and durable male polarization. These trajectories originate from the same upstream conditions but follow different logics and interact through asymmetric feedback rather than mutual determination. The paper further shows how the moralization of care generates incentive misalignment and feedback blindness, progressively decoupling moral alignment from outcome-based evaluation. Decline is conceptualized not as moral failure or institutional collapse, but as a loss of adaptive discrimination and corrective capacity under locally rational and stable equilibria. By specifying a unified causal architecture linking prosperity, selection, status competition, moralization, and decline, the framework explains why diverse downstream phenomena recurrently co-occur across societies characterized by sustained prosperity and security and why they tend to persist once established. This paper develops the theoretical core of a broader research program. Companion papers apply the framework to specific domains and institutional contexts. Note on previous versions Earlier versions of this work circulated in preliminary form on SSRN in December 2025. The present paper represents a substantial expansion and full specification of the theoretical framework.

detail.abstract:
Taxing pollutants at their marginal social costs is theoretically optimal but practically challenging when damages vary across space and technologies. Gas flaring presents exactly this problem. We quantify the climate and local health costs of flaring in the three largest U.S. flaring basins (Permian, Bakken, and Eagle Ford), showing that total social costs depend on four factors: gas composition, flare efficiency, the relative social costs of  CO2 versus methane, and population exposure to local air pollutants.

The climate damages from flaring are an order of magnitude larger than the market value of the gas. Using EPA's estimate of the social cost of greenhouse gases and detailed composition data, we estimate climate costs of flaring are $15-25/mcf  (USD2024), compared to an average real natural gas price of $2.73/mcf that year. At typical flare efficiencies, CO2 from combustion---not methane---causes the majority of climate damages from flaring. Local health expenditures vary with population density: our lower-bound estimate ranges from $1.70/mcf in the sparsely populated Bakken to $31/mcf in the more densely populated Eagle Ford---an 18-fold difference. Aggregating across the three basins, 2023 flaring imposed approximately $4 billion in climate damages and $1.6 billion in health expenditures.

These findings have direct policy implications. Methane-only regulations like the Waste Emissions Charge underprice flaring because they ignore CO2, which comprises roughly 85-95\% of total climate damages from flaring. A fully efficient policy must account for well-level variation in emissions of multiple greenhouse gases and health costs that vary across space.

detail.abstract: We present a unified theoretical framework in which all known fundamental interactions-including gravity, gauge forces, and matter-arise from a single higher-dimensional quantum structure defined by M-theory. Compactification on warped internal manifolds yields F-theory, Type IIA, and Type IIB string theories as dual descriptions in appropriate limits. Gauge symmetries, chiral matter, and fermion generations emerge from geometric singularities and flux configurations, while mass hierarchies are generated through warped localization. Building on this, we propose a Vines-Inspired Warp Drive Physics (VIWDP) mechanism, in which controlled extra-dimensional fluxes create an effective 4D warp bubble, enabling superluminal travel without violating 4D energy conditions. The combination of M/F-theory with VIWDP allows both a quantifiable unification framework and a testable approach to FTL travel, with falsifiable predictions spanning particle physics, cosmology, and gravitational phenomena.

detail.abstract: We investigate banks' risk-taking and deposit flows around first-time going concern opinions (GCOs). While GCOs may strengthen market monitoring, they are also often suspected of destabilizing banks by triggering depositor runs. Our evidence is difficult to reconcile with that concern. Uninsured deposits begin to decline several quarters before the GCO, while insured deposits increase over the same period, leaving total deposits broadly stable around the opinion. This pattern suggests that more sophisticated depositors respond to timelier information than the annual audit report and shift from uninsured to insured funding before the GCO becomes public, whereas insured retail depositors do not exhibit large-scale withdrawals around the GCO. We also document that bank risk measures rise in the quarters leading up to the GCO and then stabilize and subsequently decline after the opinion. In addition, severe enforcement actions become more likely in the post-GCO period. Taken together, these patterns are consistent with an indirect supervisory channel that may help interpret the post-GCO change in risk-taking. Overall, our findings suggest that concerns about GCOs precipitating depositor runs may be overstated in the banking setting and that systematic auditor forbearance is not clearly justified on financial stability grounds.

detail.abstract: The Paris Agreement is designed to increase climate ambition gradually through a process of ratcheting up. What is the plausible endpoint of this process? We develop a tractable integrated assessment model in which countries interact through a decentralized general equilibrium and negotiate unanimously over a global carbon budget, with all mitigation implemented via a global carbon price. We prove existence and uniqueness of a unanimous international agreement on global emissions, in which carbon pricing revenues are redistributed across countries in proportion to marginal climate damages. In a quantitative application for 154 countries, the resulting equilibrium limits global mean surface temperature change to 1.51C, at a carbon price of 320 USD/tCO2. The associated international transfers of carbon pricing revenue are progressive toward lower-income countries and amount to about 0.8% of global GDP annually - an order of magnitude larger than the Paris Agreement’s climate finance target.

detail.title: The comparative study on various taxes imposed in US state of Alaska
detail.abstract: This research examines Alaska's unique tax structure through a comprehensive quantitative analysis of petroleum and non-petroleum revenue sources from 2015-2024. Using official Alaska Department of Revenue data, this study reveals extreme revenue volatility driven by petroleum dependency, with annual tax collections fluctuating from $1.27 billion to $3.84 billion. Statistical analysis demonstrates that petroleum revenue exhibits a coefficient of variation of 46.9% compared to just 3.2% for non-petroleum sources, representing a fifteenfold difference in volatility. Inflation-adjusted analysis confirms that Alaska's fiscal challenges extend beyond nominal effects, with real revenue volatility creating governance challenges unprecedented among American states. The research quantifies Alaska's fiscal vulnerability, with petroleum taxes averaging 84% of total revenue and year-over-year growth ranging from-39% to +144%. These findings highlight critical challenges for Alaska's fiscal sustainability and provide empirical evidence supporting the urgent need for comprehensive revenue diversification strategies.

detail.abstract: Belgium’s 2016 payroll tax exemption for first-time employers triggered a sharp increase in firms hiring their first worker but little growth among larger firms. To account for this pattern, we develop and estimate a directed search model—with discrete hiring, firm heterogeneity, and endogenous entry— using Belgian microdata. The exemption reduces the high marginal cost of the first hire, enabling many previously non-hiring entrepreneurs to become employers, but most lack the productivity needed to expand beyond one worker. The model matches the post-reform size distribution and identifies the conditions under which size-dependent hiring subsidies can foster sustained firm growth.

title: The Dialectics of Fate: Stochastic Finalism and the Function of the Observer
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Dialectics of Fate: Stochastic Finalism and the Function of the Observer
detail.abstract:
The Dialectics of Fate: Stochastic Finalism and the Function of the Observer presents a systematic continuation of the theoretical framework developed in the preceding works—Anatomy of Chaos, The Dynamics of Expansion, and The Architecture of Decay. Together, these texts form a unified model of historical dynamics grounded in the thermodynamics of socio-political systems. The present work addresses the unresolved ontological problem within that framework: the role and function of the conscious subject under conditions of systemic constraint, entropy, and irreversible phase transition.

Rejecting the traditional opposition between free will and determinism, the work introduces the model of Stochastic Finalism. Within this model, historical macro-trajectories are understood as teleonomic—directed toward complexity and equilibration—without implying teleology, intention, or moral purpose. History is conceptualized as a system with a fixed terminal condition (equilibrium), while its concrete development proceeds probabilistically through stochastic events that generate critical junctions.

Within this context, the human agent is redefined as the Observer: not a moral authority or autonomous origin of action, but a functional locus through which probabilistic potential collapses into irreversible historical actuality. This role is further grounded in a four-coordinate ontology (Matter, Space, Time, Consciousness), where Consciousness functions as the axis of actualization. The transition from biological existence to historical agency—described as the Neolithic rupture—is analyzed as the activation of this coordinate, producing a permanent structural tension between biological inertia and conscious direction.

detail.title: Information About Data

detail.abstract:
Deterrence-based approaches to privacy enforcement rely on an overlooked and often false premise—that firms know what their own data practices are. There is good reason for skepticism because operational information tends to become siloed within firm subunits. Information about data management is no different. Firms may neglect to memorialize relevant information in reports for internal distribution. And even if such reports are generated, they may not be presented in a manner that is intelligible across firm constituencies.

This paper looks outside of privacy law for a solution. Recent scholarship on securities disclosures has highlighted the variety of goals that disclosures serve. While the traditional purpose of financial disclosures is to inform outside investors, the process of preparing disclosures has beneficial internal effects too. It forces firms to study their own financial health and ensures that relevant corporate units are apprised of the results. 

Mandatory disclosures about corporate data practices could have similarly beneficial effects. While some states already require firms to publish generic information about data practices to consumers, these disclosures lack basic attributes that make financial disclosures effective—they lack detail, no human signs them, and they are not filed with any state authority. Securities style disclosures hold more promise. By carefully tailoring the content, format, and required signatories of data practice disclosures, authorities could force firms to generate, translate, and  internally propagate important information about data. Firms that actually know what they are doing with data are more susceptible to efforts aimed to deter data misuse.

title: Integration of Direct Battery Recycling and Solutions to Reduce the Carbon Footprint in the Transport Industry
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Integration of Direct Battery Recycling and Solutions to Reduce the Carbon Footprint in the Transport Industry
detail.abstract:
Transport is one of the most energy-intensive and polluting sectors of the global economy: a significant proportion of modern trucks and cars still run on internal combustion engines, which produce high levels of greenhouse gas emissions and air pollutants. The very fact that there are millions of vehicles with internal combustion engines creates a system where it is increasingly difficult to achieve climate goals through full electrification alone. Another important challenge is the environmental and economic cost of extracting new resources for electric vehicle batteries, which also has a significant impact on the overall carbon balance. [5]


In the context of transport decarbonization, special attention should be paid to the difference between emissions directly during vehicle operation (tailpipe emissions) and emissions throughout the entire life cycle of technologies (life-cycle emissions). Focusing exclusively on reducing exhaust emissions creates the illusion of climate efficiency, while a significant part of the carbon footprint is actually transferred to the stages of raw material extraction, battery production, and their subsequent disposal. In the case of electric transport, this means that without well-established battery reuse and recycling systems, full electrification does not guarantee a reduction in the total carbon footprint. That is why modern approaches to decarbonization increasingly view transport not as an isolated sector, but as part of a broader material and energy system, where efficiency is determined by the balance of all stages of the life cycle.

title: Foreign Direct Investment, Efficiency, and Regional Disparities in Uganda’s Coffee Sector
affiliations: University of Science and Technology Beijing, University of Science and Technology Beijing, University of Science and Technology Beijing and University of Burundi

detail.title: Foreign Direct Investment, Efficiency, and Regional Disparities in Uganda’s Coffee Sector
detail.abstract:
Foreign direct investment (FDI) is widely promoted as a catalyst for agricultural transformation in developing countries, yet empirical evidence on its efficiency effects remains limited and mixed. This study examines the association between foreign direct investment and coffee production efficiency in Uganda, with particular attention to regional heterogeneity and policy context. Using a panel of five coffee-producing regions over the period 1995–2024, we estimate technical efficiency scores through stochastic frontier analysis and subsequently analyze their relationship with FDI exposure using fixed-effects panel regressions.
The results indicate that foreign direct investment is positively and significantly associated with coffee production efficiency, reflecting improvements in the use of existing inputs rather than expansion of cultivated area. On average, a one percent increase in FDI inflows is associated with an approximately 0.07–0.09 percent increase in production efficiency. However, these efficiency gains are unevenly distributed across regions, with stronger effects observed in relatively mature coffee-producing areas. Complementary factors including technology adoption, infrastructure, capital formation, and governance quality are also positively associated with efficiency, conditioning the magnitude of investment-related gains. In addition, the relationship between FDI and efficiency strengthens following the implementation of Uganda’s National Coffee Policy, highlighting the role of institutional reforms.
The findings suggest that while foreign investment can support efficiency-enhancing growth in smallholder-based agricultural systems, its benefits are neither automatic nor uniformly distributed. Effective investment strategies therefore require complementary public investments and institutional frameworks to promote inclusive and regionally balanced agricultural development.

title: Asset Returns, Portfolio Choice, and Proportional Wealth Taxation

detail.title: Asset Returns, Portfolio Choice, and Proportional Wealth Taxation
detail.abstract: We analyse the effect of a proportional wealth tax on asset returns, portfolio choice, and asset pricing in a partial equilibrium setting. The tax is levied annually on the market value of all holdings at a uniform rate. We show that such a tax is economically equivalent to the government acquiring a proportional stake in the investor's portfolio each period — a form of risk sharing in which expected wealth and risk are reduced by the same factor, while the return per share is unaffected. This multiplicative separability between the tax factor and the return realisation drives four main results. First, the coefficient of variation of wealth is invariant to the tax rate, since the tax reduces expected wealth and risk by the same proportion. Second, the optimal portfolio weights — and in particular the tangency portfolio — are independent of the tax rate. Third, the wealth tax is orthogonal to portfolio choice: in discrete time it induces a homothetic contraction of the opportunity set in the mean–standard deviation plane that preserves the Sharpe ratio of every portfolio. Fourth, both taxed and untaxed investors are willing to pay the same price per share for any asset. The results are derived first under geometric Brownian motion and then generalised to any return distribution in the location-scale family. A complementary Modigliani-Miller analysis, treating the tax claim as a separate security, confirms pricing neutrality and identifies an inconsistency in the existing literature regarding the discount rate used for after-tax cash flows. Imposing the Capital Asset Pricing Model as a special case confirms that after-tax betas equal pre-tax betas and the security market line contracts uniformly by (1 − τ_w); under CRRA preferences, general-equilibrium returns and prices are unchanged. This resolves an error in Fama (2021), who overstates the price effect by adding the wealth tax to the cost of capital without adjusting the discount rate. The neutrality results depend on three conditions that are commonly violated in practice: universal taxation at market value, frictionless markets, and dividend consumption. We formalise three channels through which relaxing these conditions breaks neutrality — book-value taxation, liquidity frictions, and dividend extraction — and show that they have opposing effects on asset prices.

title: A Chicken-and-Egg Problem: Profits and Inflation after COVID-19

detail.title: A Chicken-and-Egg Problem: Profits and Inflation after COVID-19
detail.abstract: In 2022, the contribution of unit profits to domestic price pressures in the Euro area more than doubled relative to its historical average. This increase was uneven across industries and particularly pronounced in upstream sectors. While profits have attracted growing attention as a potential driver of inflation, the existing literature has not examined their role within a fully structural macroeconomic framework alongside a broad set of competing price pressures. In this paper, I propose a unified Bayesian VAR framework to disentangle how profits have affected inflation in the Euro area, focusing on the period after the pandemic. The results show that while demand and energy prices initially drove inflation, profits in upstream companies further amplified price pressures, thereby delaying the return of inflation to the 2% target. In the labor-capital distribution debate, profits contribute about one-third more to price pressures than wages. Moreover, firms more than offset by a factor of four the losses they incurred during the pandemic. Overall, the findings suggest that increasing concentration in key sectors poses a material risk to price stability and warrants close monitoring.

title: Expenditure Smoothing under Balanced Budget Rules
affiliations: University of Houston - Department of Economics, , Indiana University Bloomington, University of Houston, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Expenditure Smoothing under Balanced Budget Rules
detail.abstract: An increasing number of countries use balanced budget rules (BBRs) to control government debt, with the potential cost that BBRs constrain the governments’ ability to smooth public expenditures. We find that U.S. state governments, despite having BBRs, smooth expenditures using savings. This is accomplished via substantial cash balances held by agencies outside of the General Fund with only a minor contribution from dedicated “rainy day” funds. We estimate a state government discount rate using a buffer stock model, fitted to fiscal data consolidated over all agencies, and find that expenditures are smoothed as if guided by a planner with a discount rate similar to that typically found for consumers.

title: Five Objections to Commodification
affiliations: Harvard Law School

detail.title: Five Objections to Commodification
detail.abstract: In free markets, countless goods may be bought and sold. What was once not traded on markets-for example, access to public parks or sexual and reproductive capacitiesmight be turned into a commodity. Time and again, allowing things to be bought and sold increases both autonomy and welfare. Still, there are pervasive objections to commodification. The first set of objections points to illicit preferences and values and the importance of delegitimating, or not legitimating, those preferences and values (for example, employers cannot "buy" the right to engage in sexual harassment). A second set of objections involves collective action problems: commodification might create such problems (consider the right to vote). A third set of objections invokes equality (as, for example, when people reject the idea that access to public parks should be allocated on the basis of willingness to pay). A fourth set of objections points to information failures and behavioral biases, potentially producing blocked exchanges. A fifth set of objections emphasizes what may be the corrosive effects of commodification on the goods in questions (consider prostitution). detail.abstract: The determination of death is a foundational clinical practice, yet the transition from biological presence to administrative record is fraught with friction. This Viewpoint argues that the modern clinical and legal setting is a site of conflict between divergent global definitions of death: medical, legal, economic, statistical, religious, and coronial. Governed by national statutes and international registries, these systems have created a Kafkaesque labyrinth where the administrative record often supersedes biological reality. Drawing on Giorgio Agamben's concept of "Bare Life" and the literary frameworks of Franz Kafka, we analyse the "Bureaucratic Demise" (the moment when the file takes precedence over the person). We examine global cases of jurisdictional death, the absurdity of registry errors, and the administrative paralysis of the coronial system to highlight the dissonance between the messy reality of the dying body and the rigid requirements of the global bureaucracy. Finally, we propose narrative medicine as a humble, human-centric alternative to multidisciplinary reductionism.

detail.abstract:
The brutal conflict between Hamas and Israel convulsed higher education. Student protestors have demanded that university endowments "divest" from Israel. University leaders have largely resisted those demands on grounds of fiduciary obligation, institutional neutrality, or both. In response, protestors have pointed to prior instances of purported divestment. Confusion abounds over the applicable fiduciary principles and the scope of prior divestments. This paper synthesizes the law and finance of endowment divestment and applies that analysis to past divestments and present divestment demands. 

We show that under prevailing law endowment divestment for nonfinancial reasons is permissible only if: (1) the divestment is consistent with the university's charitable purpose of research and education, and (2) the divestment's effect on the portfolio is reasonable in light of that purpose. Applied to the current state of university endowment management, this is a highly restrictive standard. The charitable purpose of most secular universities is research and education, full stop. Moreover, contemporary endowment practice relies on external managers, making a divestment today more costly to implement than in the past. Under current endowment practice, therefore, even a de minimis divestment, whether from Israel or otherwise, would likely be a fiduciary breach, potentially exposing university trustees to out-of-pocket damages for any resulting loss to the endowment. 

We also examine current divestment policies and purported prior divestments, including South Africa under apartheid, tobacco, the Darfur war, and fossil fuels. Consistent with our legal analysis, but contrary to conventional wisdom, we find that universities have generally not engaged in broad divestments, not even from South Africa under apartheid. Instead, most large university endowments adhere to a narrow divestment policy for "moral abhorrence" that has rarely been invoked. We show that a divestment for moral abhorrence could pass fiduciary muster as consistent with the public benefit principle of charity law if supported by a clear public policy established by confirmatory governmental actions.

detail.abstract: State capacity, the ability to achieve policy goals and provide public goods, is a central concept in contemporary political economy. National defense is the textbook case of a public good requiring state provision. Analysis of defense provision, however, assumes that the state possesses the means and the incentives to serve public interest. We reconsider the meaning of state capacity by examining the institutional context surrounding the provision of national defense and the militaryindustrial complex. Because defense is supplied outside the market, decisions about scope and quality are inherently political and shaped by information and incentive constraints that differ from market settings. We show how the instruments of defense provision create channels for special interests, so that a capable state risks becoming a captured one. We argue that this dynamic is not simply unidirectional capture but a reciprocal process of political capitalism, in which political and economic elites jointly produce privilege.

detail.abstract: This paper utilizes data from Chinese A-share listed companies and, based on the limited attention theory, reexamines the impact of data asset disclosure on capital market pricing efficiency. The study finds that the economic consequences of data asset disclosure are not static but exhibit a significant marginal decreasing feature as the overall market disclosure level rises. Specifically, when the overall market disclosure level is low, corporate disclosure of data asset information can significantly reduce stock price synchronization and enhance capital market pricing efficiency by increasing the supply of idiosyncratic information, enhancing information diffusion, and accelerating information integration. However, with the recent widespread disclosure behavior, there is no evidence that the above mechanisms remain effective. Further analysis indicates that disclosure behavior can maintain its positive effect only when the overall market disclosure level of data assets is low, and the firm's disclosed idiosyncratic information is relatively limited, the information dissemination environment is favorable, or institutional investor attention is not excessively diffused. This paper expands the boundaries of the limited attention theory, extending the research perspective to the dimension of the dispersion of investor attention by homogenized information, and reveals the value dilution problem faced by data asset information disclosure in the context of universalization.

detail.abstract: Using confidential supervisory data, we measure disagreement among bank syndicate lenders about borrowers’ credit risk by exploiting dispersion in probability-of-default (PD) estimates that banks report to the Federal Reserve for the same borrower-loan pair. Consistent with theory, disagreement is greater for larger loans and syndicates. At origination, loans with higher disagreement carry significantly higher spreads, even after controlling for borrower and loan risk characteristics. Although disagreement does not affect the number of covenants, it lowers the likelihood that contracts include performance-pricing provisions, consistent with lenders seeking to avoid future coordination frictions. After origination, banks with more pessimistic PD assessments are more likely to exit the syndicate, and greater disagreement lowers the probability of loan amendments following both positive and negative shocks to borrower fundamentals. However, successful renegotiations narrow subsequent disagreement. Overall, our evidence shows that within-syndicate coordination frictions shape loan pricing, contract design, syndicate composition, and renegotiation outcomes.

detail.abstract: Green consumerism has gained huge momentum in sustainability research and policy discussions as environmental risks and climate change intensify. Over past twenty years researchers have conducted study into how climate perceptions, ecological awareness and sustainability norms affect consumer behavior. Despite the fast growth of this field a thorough overview of its ideas and research trends and aspects is still lacking. This study provides a bibliometric analysis of global research on green consumerism in relation to climate change from 2000 to 2025. Using Scopus as the main database we identified over 1,000 relevant publications through a structured Boolean search. These were screened using specific inclusion criteria and analyzed with VOS viewer and the Bibliometric (Biblioshiny) R package. The analysis shows a significant increase in publications after 2015 indicating rising urgency around climate issues and the impact of sustainable consumption movements. Science mapping techniques like keyword co-occurrence, co-citation and bibliographic coupling reveal four main clusters that are green purchase intention models, climate beliefs and environmental attitudes, sustainable lifestyles and low carbon consumption and circular economy and green marketing strategies. Thematic evolution analysis indicates a shift from traditional behavioral theories (TPB, VBN) in earlier years to modern themes like carbon neutrality, climate anxiety, eco innovation and circular consumption in the 2020s. This study establishes a future agenda for increasing research on climate-focused consumer behavior, improves understanding of global knowledge development and identifies emerging research areas. Researchers, decision-makers and companies can use these insights to adapt to shifting sustainability demands.

detail.abstract:
The law endows corporations and other business organizations with the awesome power of perpetual life—unless the charter expressly provides for a certain duration, such as ten years. But does anyone ever actually choose limited life? Why would they?

This article reveals that limited-life business entities—finite ventures—play a significant and underappreciated role in modern commerce. Private equity and venture capital funds, SPACs, and insurance syndicates are all organized with a limited lifespan.Their motivation? This article claims that limited life is a valuable, but often overlooked, tool for ameliorating agency costs: the managers of a finite venture know they must produce results by the end of the term—their future career prospects depend on it—so they have an incentive to be diligent and loyal.

Even so, limited life has drawbacks—and perpetual life has benefits of its own—so the trick is to know when to use it. To guide decision-makers, this article identifies key factors that weigh in favor of or against finite structure. It closes by proposing novel applications of limited life as a tool of corporate governance—inviting scholars and practitioners alike to rethink the assumption of corporate immortality.

Purpose:
Consumer behaviour of Millennials and Generation Z has been coined as “doom spending.” The uncertainty driven by anxiety on internal and external levels has given a behavioural nudge towards consumerism. Consequently, the researchers investigate the transformation in this spending behaviour. The objective of the article is to explore the drivers of doom spending and examine its psychological and behavioural aspects among Indian consumers.

Design:
Survey data was collected from 200 respondents in the age range of 20 to 50. Data was collected on three dimensions of spending by consumer- mental, emotional, and social. Additionally, in-depth understanding of these dimensions was received by collecting qualitative data. The data analysis included carrying out Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) with Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for arriving at the optimum variables within each dimension. Furthermore, content analysis was performed on the qualitative data set.

Findings:
The key results of the study reflect the consumption behaviour of both the generations inclining towards luxury spending predominantly influenced by peers. Moreover, it was also found that the external environment in the form of social and digital media enhances the internal parameters of sensitivity, stress, and impulsion towards consumerism. The key insights are explained by Stimulus-Organism-Response (SOR) model. The qualitative finding reveals ‘fear of future’ and ‘consumption as catharsis’ as major arguments for spending behaviour.

Originality:
This unique research demonstrates behavioural contradictions in fulfilment of SDG 12 of ‘responsible consumption’. The implications are relevant for policymakers to nudge the production towards sustainable spending of Millennials and Generation Z.

detail.abstract: Which startups can attract the talent they need to grow? We argue that worker preferences over which problems to solve shape labor supply to early-stage firms. In male-dominated labor markets, startups focused on women may struggle to recruit, especially for critical, male-dominated roles like engineering and senior leadership. We combine observational data on over 52,000 U.S. high-potential startups with a pre-registered field experiment. Linking startups to over 2.5 million worker histories, we find that female-focused startups employ fewer workers: a one standard deviation increase in a startup’s female-focus predicts 11% fewer male employees. To isolate worker preferences, we run a field experiment where we randomize the startup idea itself, thereby developing a new experimental paradigm to causally identify how the nature of an idea matters. We built a job-search platform recruiting real tech job seekers in a within-subject design, where each participant evaluates 15 startup ideas, each randomized to be more or less female-focused. Crucially, our experiment is incentive-compatible, because participants’ evaluations affect which real job postings our platform subsequently recommends to them. Male job seekers are 6.8 percentage points less likely to apply to female-focused startups than other startups, a 10% decrease from baseline. Offsetting the male penalty would require approximately $47,000 in additional yearly compensation. Our findings demonstrate that who benefits from an idea is an important nonpecuniary job attribute shaping talent acquisition, potentially helping explain why ventures serving women grow more slowly.

detail.abstract: This study examines how the COVID-19 pandemic, as a disruptive external shock, has reshaped organizational practices, with particular emphasis on changes in work design and compensation strategies. Drawing on a unique dataset of over 1.8 million online job postings from Chinese publicly listed firms, we employed a large language model to systematically quantify work design characteristics. Using a difference-indifferences approach, we found that the pandemic significantly enhanced skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy, feedback, and work-from-home feasibility. Notably, these effects varied by occupational nonroutineness: occupations with high nonroutineness exhibited larger increases in task significance but smaller increases in other work design characteristics. Moreover, work design characteristics mediated the relationship between the pandemic and salaries, though these indirect effects were attenuated for nonroutine occupations. Additionally, we observed post-pandemic adjustments in firms' compensation, including notable declines in performance-related pay and insurance benefits, accompanied by increases in subsidies. These findings provide new insights into how organizations redesign work and adjust compensation strategies in response to large-scale external shocks.

detail.abstract: This working paper offers a hypothesis-generating reinterpretation of Father Marc Marie de Rotz’s (1840–1914) initiatives in Sotome, Nagasaki, through the combined lenses of relational (reciprocal) philanthropy and ecosystem-oriented institutional design. Focusing on the Shitsu Relief Institute (est. 1883) as a coordinating hub, it shows how livelihood support and skills training were bundled with education, basic healthcare, and community infrastructure to address institutional gaps in an isolated coastal community. Drawing on relational grantmaking (e.g., Petzinger & Jung, 2024), co-production theory, and institutional work, the paper conceptualizes these practices as institutional stitching: (1) sustained co-presence that enables trust and local knowledge circulation; (2) beneficiary co-production that transforms beneficiaries into local agents; (3) multi-domain coupling that creates resilient pathways among livelihoods, learning, and care; and (4) long-term repair and maintenance that stabilizes emerging rules, capacities, and legitimacy. The paper contributes an integrative concept linking relational mechanisms (reciprocity, trust, power-sharing) with ecosystem mechanisms (cross-domain linkages, spatial configuration, and implementation capacity), and concludes with implications for contemporary place-based care ecosystems and Ecosystem for New Philanthropy (ENP)-oriented design.

title: The Institutionalization Revelation: How ETFs Exposed Bitcoin's Speculative Nature within the Debasement Trade
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: The Institutionalization Revelation: How ETFs Exposed Bitcoin's Speculative Nature within the Debasement Trade
detail.abstract: The post-2020 global financial landscape, characterized by unprecedented monetary and fiscal expansion, has given rise to the "debasement trade" narrative, the investment thesis that excessive government debt growth devalues fiat currencies relative to scarce assets. Within this framework, Bitcoin has occupied a conceptual dual identity: as a digital monetary commodity akin to gold (the "digital gold" hypothesis) and as a speculative technology growth asset. The January 2024 approval of U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) created a natural experiment to test whether institutional adoption transforms or reveals an asset's fundamental characteristics within the debasement trade framework. Analyzing daily returns from January 2020 to January 2026 across five asset classes, this study examines Bitcoin's behavior before and after ETF approval. Contrary to transformation theories, results indicate institutionalization weakened Bitcoin's debasement hedge properties (beta changed from-1.61 to +0.63, p<.01), failed to increase its correlation with gold (0.156 to 0.091, p=.219), and diminished its optimal portfolio weight from 31.2% to 2.9%. Bitcoin's volatility decreased (74.6% to 47.6% annualized) but remained characteristic of speculative assets, and correlation with the S&P 500 showed no significant increase (0.378 to 0.362, p=.736). These findings support an "institutionalization revelation" hypothesis: rather than transforming Bitcoin into a monetary asset, institutional participation reveals its true nature as a speculative technology innovation. The results challenge the "digital gold" narrative within the debasement trade framework and suggest Bitcoin's value proposition remains technological rather than monetary, with implications for portfolio construction, risk management, and financial regulation.

title: Administrative Justice and the Boards of Appeal of EU Agencies
